origin: Five settings come from the pre-registration (target, 90% range, global CQR calibration, 10 folds of 50 km blocks) or from the EDA (log target, a tree model for skewed and collinear inputs). The LightGBM settings were chosen once and never tuned or documented; section 3 checks whether that matters.
repro: Refitting the primary model from the data on disk reproduces the published predictions exactly: expected counts and lower bounds agree to floating-point precision and all 510 flags are identical. Together with the reproduced tract table (eda/03), the whole chain from public data to published flags is reproducible.
grid: Coverage stays at 90.0% in every variant, because conformal calibration enforces it whatever the model. Fit and skill barely move with the LightGBM settings, the block size or the number of folds (R² 0.922-0.928, lift 4.6-5.7). What matters is the inputs: without the ACS housing-type columns R² falls from 0.926 to 0.845, the range widens by 43%, lift drops from 5.1 to 3.6 and three quarters of the flagged tracts change; with only housing units, population and land it is worse again (R² 0.778, lift 3.2). The LODES job inputs matter little for buildings (they were added for places).
seedfloor: Changing nothing but the random seed already changes about a quarter of the flagged tracts (overlap 0.73). Every hyperparameter, block-size and fold-count variant falls within about that noise (overlap 0.65-0.90); only removing inputs moves far beyond it (0.25-0.27). So the untuned LightGBM settings are not a weakness, but individual tract flags are noisy: the paper should treat a flag as a probabilistic screen, and aggregate results (coverage, lift, group rates) are the robust quantities. Averaging flags over several seeds would make tract-level lists more stable.
01_summary: The model is reproducible, its calibration does not depend on its settings, and its skill depends on the inputs (the ACS housing-type columns above all), not on the LightGBM tuning. The main caveat is that a quarter of the flagged tracts change with the random seed alone, so tract-level flags should be read as a screen rather than a verdict.
dist: Out-of-fold residuals are centred on zero (mean -0.006, sd 0.21 log points, about ±21%) and only 2% exceed ±0.5. They are skewed to the left in every region except eastern WA: large shortfalls are more common than large surpluses, which is the shape the method looks for. Eastern WA is shifted the other way (mean +0.04): the model under-predicts its building counts.
calib: Coverage is 0.89-0.93 by region, but it is not uniform across tract types. Flags concentrate in small tracts: 14% of tracts in the smallest decile of expected count are flagged against about 4-5% in the middle and 1% in the largest, because a few missing buildings are a large share of a small count. Eastern WA has the opposite problem: almost no flags (0.2%) and 11% of tracts above the upper bound. Global CQR guarantees 90% on average, not within each size class; a size-stratified (Mondrian) calibration would even this out, and this conditional miscalibration should be stated alongside the flag results.
drift: The residuals barely drift with any input: across deciles of housing units, land area, density, mobile-home, group-quarters and vacancy shares and jobs, mean residuals stay within ±0.05 log points (about ±5%). The largest pattern is a slight over-prediction in the smallest-area tracts (-0.05). The model has no strong systematic misfit along any structural dimension.
moran: Errors do cluster in space: Moran's I of the building residuals is 0.09-0.18 in every region, all significant (permutation p = 0.005), and similar for places. Flags cluster more weakly (0.06-0.08; none in eastern WA, where there are almost no flags). Neighbouring tracts share unmeasured local factors, such as mapping campaigns or building styles, so random cross-validation would overstate accuracy, which is why the model is cross-fitted over spatial blocks.
decay: The residual correlation is highest between tracts within a few kilometres (about 0.1-0.2), falls below 0.03 by 25-45 km and is near zero beyond 50 km in four regions; eastern WA keeps a small correlation (about 0.03) out to roughly 60 km. The 50 km spatial blocks are therefore large enough to separate training and test tracts almost everywhere, and the 25 km and 100 km variants in 01 confirm that the block size changes nothing material.
maps: Flags (circles) are not spread evenly: they bunch in the dense clusters of small tracts that make up the metropolitan areas (most visibly in south-central Texas, and along the urban corridors of Maricopa and eastern Oklahoma), while rural tracts have fewer flags and more scattered residuals. This matches section 2 (flags concentrate in small tracts) and section 4 (short-range clustering). These maps use the 2026-08 release, so the 2026-10 San Antonio drop is not in them. The maps show tract centroids without a basemap, so they locate patterns roughly, not individual neighbourhoods.
02_summary: The building model's errors are small, centred and without strong drift, and their spatial correlation dies out within the 50 km block size. Two caveats belong in the paper: the 90% range is not equally calibrated across tract sizes (flags concentrate in small tracts, almost none in eastern WA), and errors cluster spatially at short range, so neighbouring flags are not independent evidence.
